Last Time: Classification¶

  • Logit is one node with a sigmoid, trained on cross entropy
  • SoftMax turns a network's raw outputs into probabilities that add to 1, and ArgMax reads off the answer
  • K nearest neighbors classifies by a vote among the closest training points, and with many inputs nobody is near
  • An image has thousands of inputs. Today the classifier is a network again, with the SoftMax output from lecture 12

Where We Are Going¶

  • Two 6 by 6 drawings, an O and an X, and a computer that has to say which is which
  • Three reasons an ordinary network struggles with pictures
  • A filter slides across the picture, then ReLU, then max pooling, then the network from lecture 10
  • Every number by hand on the O, on the X, and on an X nudged one pixel to the right
  • Color: three grids instead of one
  • Handwritten digits off old forms, trained live
  • A case study: poverty measured from satellite pictures

Three Problems With Pictures¶

A friend plays tic-tac-toe against the computer and can never remember whether the game starts with an X or an O. So every game, the computer has to work out which letter was drawn.

Zoom in on the screen and each letter is a grid of pixels. Here they are 6 pixels by 6, white or black. Write a white pixel as 0 and a black one as 1 and each drawing is 36 numbers.

Problem 1: Too Many Weights¶

  • Stack the 36 pixels into a column of input nodes and connect them to one hidden node: 36 weights, each one found by backpropagation
  • Every extra hidden node is another 36
  • A 100 by 100 picture is still small, and it is 10,000 weights per hidden node. This does not scale

Problem 2: A One Pixel Shift¶

  • Train on the O on the left. Then show it the same O drawn one pixel to the right
  • Every one of the 36 input nodes now holds a different number. Nothing in the network says the answer is still O

Problem 3: Neighbors Look Alike¶

  • In a real photo a dark pixel sits among dark pixels and a light pixel among light ones. Nearby pixels are correlated
  • Feeding the pixels in one node at a time throws that away. It would be good to use it

What a CNN Does About All Three¶

  • Fewer input nodes than pixels
  • Tolerance to small shifts in where the drawing sits
  • Uses the correlations between neighboring pixels

Here is the machine, numbers and all. It looks like a lot. Each piece gets its own slide.

Step by Step¶

A convolutional neural network, CNN for short, in the smallest version that does the job: one filter, one bias, ReLU, one round of max pooling, and a four input network on the end. Every number below can be checked by hand.

The Filter¶

  • A filter, also called a kernel, is a small square of numbers, commonly 3 by 3
  • Its nine numbers are weights.
  • They start random, and backpropagation sets them
  • This one ends up as a diagonal stroke, because a diagonal stroke is what tells an O from an X

Overlay, Multiply, Add¶

  • Lay the filter over the top left corner of the picture

  • Multiply each overlapping pair and add the nine products: 3

  • Fancy name: a sum of products is a dot product.

  • A convolution is an operation that combines two functions or arrays to produce a third one.

    • By computing the dot product between the input and the filter, the filter is convolved with the input, thus Convolutional Neural Network.

Add a Bias, Write It Down¶

  • Add a bias, also learned by backpropagation. Here it is −2, so 3 − 2 = 1
  • The 1 goes into the top left cell of the feature map

Slide It One Pixel¶

  • Move the filter one column to the right and do it again: dot product 1, plus the bias, −1
  • How far it moves each step is the stride. One here. Bigger pictures often use 2 or 3

Keep Going Until the Map Is Full¶

  • Four positions across and four rows down: 16 dot products, 16 cells
  • The filter cannot hang over the edge, so a 6 by 6 picture and a 3 by 3 filter give a 4 by 4 map

The Finished Feature Map¶

  • The picture went in, the filter went over it, a bias was added, and a 4 by 4 map came out
  • Two cells hold a 1: the two places where the filter matched the drawing perfectly

Each Cell Remembers Its Neighborhood¶

  • Every cell of the map came from a 3 by 3 block of neighboring pixels, read together.
    • This takes advantage of correlations in the image
  • The 1 at the bottom right of the map is the diagonal stroke at the bottom right of the O

ReLU¶

  • Run the map through ReLU from lecture 10: negatives become 0, positives stay what they were
  • Two cells survive, the two perfect matches

Max Pooling¶

  • A second filter, with no weights to learn: look at a 2 by 2 block and keep the largest value
  • It moves so the blocks never overlap, stride 2, so the 4 by 4 map becomes 2 by 2
  • Keeping the average instead is average pooling. Classifiers mostly use max

Where the Filter Matched Best¶

  • The 1 at the top left of the pooled grid came from the top left block of the map, and that block came from the top left quarter of the picture, where the filter sat on the stroke
  • So max pooling keeps where the filter did its best job, and forgets where inside the block that was. That is the shift tolerance, and it gets its own slide

From Grid to Column¶

  • Read the pooled grid off as a column: 1, 0, 0, 1
  • Four input nodes. The picture had 36 pixels

Into an Ordinary Network¶

  • Four inputs, one hidden node with ReLU, two outputs: one for O and one for X
  • The weights and biases below were found by backpropagation on drawings of both letters, lecture 11 again
  • The printed version of this example has 1.6 for the hidden bias and −0.45 for the weight into X. The published errata correct them to 0.97 and 1.33, and only the corrected values give the outputs on the next slides

The O Comes Out as an O¶

  • Sum: (1 × −0.8) + (0 × −0.07) + (0 × 0.2) + (1 × 0.17) + 0.97 = 0.34
  • ReLU leaves 0.34, since it is positive
  • O output: 0.34 × −1.33 + 1.45 = 1.00. X output: 0.34 × 1.33 − 0.45 = 0.00

Now the X¶

  • Same filter, same bias, same weights. Only the drawing changes
  • The feature map, ReLU and pooling give 0, 1, 1, 0, the sum is 1.10, and the outputs are 0 for O and 1 for X

36 Inputs Became 4¶

  • Problem 1: the network on the end has 4 inputs and 4 weights into its hidden node, not 36. Bigger pictures use more filters and more pooling, and the count stays small
  • Problem 3: the filter reads a 3 by 3 block at a time, so neighbors are used together
  • Problem 2 is next

The X Nudged One Pixel Right¶

  • Shift the X one pixel to the right. Every cell of the feature map changes
  • After ReLU and pooling the column is 0, 1, 1, 1, one cell away from the X's 0, 1, 1, 0
  • Outputs −0.24 for O and 1.24 for X. Still an X. (The source rounds these to −0.2 and 1.23)
  • SoftMax from lecture 12 would turn the pair into probabilities, and ArgMax would just say X

Bigger CNNs Are More of the Same¶

  • Real ones use many filters, so one picture becomes many feature maps, and they run convolution, ReLU and pooling again on those maps before the ordinary network
  • Every piece is still a filter, an activation and a pooling step
  • Each layer's maps are the next layer's picture, with as many channels as there were filters...

Training the Filter¶

  • Start the filter and every weight at random and train on the four drawings above with cross entropy, lecture 12
  • A few hundred steps of gradient descent. The filter that comes out need not be the diagonal one, since more than one filter separates these drawings
O           P(O) 1.00   P(X) 0.00
X           P(O) 0.00   P(X) 1.00
X shifted   P(O) 0.00   P(X) 1.00
O shifted   P(O) 1.00   P(X) 0.00

Color: Three Grids Instead of One¶

  • A black and white pixel is one number. A color pixel is three: how much red, green and blue light, each from 0 to 1
  • White is 1, 1, 1. Black is 0, 0, 0. A red stroke is 1, 0, 0
  • So a color picture is three 6 by 6 grids, called channels, and the same O drawn in red looks like this

The Red O Is Invisible in Red¶

  • The red channel is all 1s. The drawing is there as missing green and missing blue
  • A filter that reads only one channel would never see a red stroke on a white page in the red channel. It has to read all three

A Color Filter Is Three Grids Too¶

  • One 3 by 3 per channel: 27 weights, plus one bias
  • Overlay all three at once, multiply, and add all 27 products: still one number, into one feature map
  • Worked at the top left: the red channel's nine products add to 3, green's to 0, blue's to 0. Total 3

Why Keep the Color¶

  • Turn the page gray, one number per pixel, and a red O and a blue O become the same drawing. No filter can tell them apart after that
  • With three channels the filter above gives 3 on the red O and −3 on the blue O
  • Shape lives in all three channels. Color lives in how they differ. A filter can read either
color filter at the top left:   red O +3    blue O -3
gray filter at the top left:    red O +2    blue O +2

When Gray Loses the Drawing¶

  • Draw the O in a red whose gray level matches the page: page 0.5, 0.5, 0.5 and stroke 1, 0.25, 0.25. Both average to 0.5
  • Turn that gray and the page is blank. The filter from the first half gives the same number at every position
  • The three channels still see it: the red channel reads 1 against 0.5, and green and blue read 0.25 against 0.5. The color filter gives 1.5 on the stroke and −1.5 off it
  • When the data do not need color, gray is fine and it is a third of the numbers. The handwritten digits coming up are gray for that reason
gray filter, every position:   [1.5]
color filter, top left (on the stroke) +1.5,   middle (off the stroke) -1.5

A Photo Has Channels Too¶

  • Any color photo is three grids the size of the picture. A 600 by 512 photo is 921,600 numbers
  • The three channels of one photo, each shown in its own color
shape of the photo: (600, 512, 3)    numbers: 921600

In PyTorch: in_channels=3¶

  • nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=1, kernel_size=3): the weight tensor is 1 filter by 3 channels by 3 by 3, the 27 numbers from two slides ago
  • out_channels is how many filters. Each filter makes one feature map, and that count is the next layer's in_channels
  • A color picture goes in with shape (batch, 3, rows, columns)
red O    input shape (1, 3, 6, 6)   feature map top left +3   whole map min -3 max +3
blue O   input shape (1, 3, 6, 6)   feature map top left -3   whole map min -3 max -3
weight shape: (1, 3, 3, 3)   weights: 27  bias: 1

Handwritten Digits Off Old Forms¶

  • Census pages, tax rolls and ledgers were filled in by hand. Turning them into data means reading digits off scans, millions of them
  • The standard training set: 70,000 scanned digits, each 28 by 28 pixels, each labeled 0 to 9
  • A pixel is now a gray level from 0 to 1, not just 0 or 1. The filter arithmetic does not care
training on 10000 digits, testing on 2000

The Same Machine, Four Filters¶

  • nn.Conv2d(1, 4, 3): four 3 by 3 filters and four biases, 40 numbers. Four 26 by 26 feature maps
  • ReLU, then 2 by 2 max pooling: four 13 by 13 maps, 676 numbers
  • nn.Linear(676, 10): ten raw outputs, SoftMax and cross entropy from lecture 12
  • 6,810 parameters in all. A dense first layer with 676 hidden nodes on the 784 pixels would need 530,660
parameters: 6810
a dense layer, 784 pixels to 676 hidden nodes: 530660

Train It¶

  • 10,000 training digits, 2,000 held back for testing. Five passes over the training set in batches of 50, Adam steps from lecture 10
  • Watch the share of the held back digits read correctly climb
pass 1   held back digits read correctly: 87.4%
pass 2   held back digits read correctly: 90.1%
pass 3   held back digits read correctly: 90.3%
pass 4   held back digits read correctly: 91.5%
pass 5   held back digits read correctly: 91.2%

The Four Filters It Learned¶

  • Nobody drew these. Backpropagation found four 3 by 3 patterns that help tell the ten digits apart
  • Below each filter, its feature map for one 3: where in the drawing that pattern was found

The Ones It Gets Wrong¶

  • The first ten held back digits it misread, with what it said and what was written
  • Most are the ones a person would hesitate over too. The next slide adds a second round of convolution and pooling
misread 176 of 2000

A Second Round¶

  • The four 13 by 13 maps are a picture with four channels. So run another set of filters over them, each filter 3 by 3 by 4, then ReLU and pooling again
  • Eight filters, then sixteen: the picture shrinks to 5 by 5 by 16, 400 numbers into the last layer. 5,258 parameters, fewer than the one round version, since the dense layer got smaller
  • Trained the same way on the same digits, eight passes. With all 60,000 and more passes this design reads above 99 percent

Case Study: Poverty From Satellite Pictures¶

Jean, Burke, Xie, Davis, Lobell and Ermon (2016), "Combining satellite imagery and machine learning to predict poverty", Science 353, 790 to 794.

  • Between 2000 and 2010, 39 of 59 African countries ran fewer than two surveys that could measure poverty nationally, and 14 ran none
  • Night lights from space track economic activity at the country level, but below the poverty line they are dim everywhere and barely vary
  • Daytime satellite pictures are free and cover everything. Nobody has labeled them with incomes

Three Steps¶

  1. Start from a CNN already trained on ImageNet, a million labeled everyday photos. Its filters already know edges, textures and shapes
  2. Keep training it to predict night light brightness from the daytime picture of the same place. Plenty of labels, all free
  3. Throw away the last layer. The numbers the CNN computes for a village's pictures go into a ridge regression, lecture 7, on survey consumption or assets. Ridge because there are many more features than surveyed villages
  • Consumption from the World Bank's LSMS surveys in four countries, asset wealth from DHS surveys in five. Scored by cross validation, lecture 6

What It Found¶

  • Consumption per head, four countries, cross validated: 37 to 55 percent of the variation across villages explained
  • Asset wealth, five countries: 55 to 75 percent
  • One model pooled across countries: 44 to 59 percent
  • Among villages below the poverty line it beats night lights in 81 percent of trials; below three times the line, in 99.5 percent
  • Rwanda assets: r² of 0.75, against 0.62 from a study that used mobile phone records, which are proprietary

What the Filters Look At¶

  • Four of the trained filters light up on urban areas, farmland, water and roads. Nobody told the network to look for those; they are what predicts night lights
  • A placebo: shuffle the pictures among villages and refit, 1,000 times. The r² collapses every time. The pictures carry the information, not the fitting
  • Roofing material and distance to a town, which surveyors ask about, are things a daytime picture can see

From Prediction to a Treatment Effect¶

Ratledge, Cadamuro, de la Cuesta, Stigler and Burke (2022), Nature 611, 491 to 495.

  • A ResNet-18 CNN reads Landsat tiles, 224 by 224 pixels by 6 bands, trained on 27,174 villages in 25 countries, 641,621 surveyed households. Held out r² 0.63
  • The predicted wealth becomes the outcome: Uganda's grid expansion, 209 villages electrified and 3,235 not, a prediction for every village every year from 2006 to 2016
  • Grid access raised village asset wealth by up to 0.15 standard deviations, estimated with panel methods that build each electrified village's counterfactual from the ones still waiting
  • The CNN is a measuring device. The identification is the same job as lectures 15 to 19. Lecture 18's appendix runs the reverse, pictures as controls

Another Application: Reading Body Motion¶

The satellite model slid a filter across a picture. But a filter does not care what the axis means. Slide it across time instead of space and the same machine reads motion.

Here is a published example: Yang and colleagues used a convolutional neural network to recognize everyday activities — opening a door, drinking from a cup, a tennis swing — from the signals of body-worn motion sensors.

Yang, Nguyen, San, Li & Krishnaswamy, Deep Convolutional Neural Networks on Multichannel Time Series for Human Activity Recognition (IJCAI 2015).

The Picture Is Now a Motion Clip¶

A body-worn accelerometer measures how a limb speeds up and slows down, and a gyroscope measures how it turns. Read them many times a second and every instant is a handful of numbers.

Take a short window and you have a grid of time by channels — one row per sensor axis. That grid is the picture now.

An activity is a small shape in time, and it has to be told apart from the other activities — and from the dominant "Null" class, the long stretches when nothing of interest is happening.

Same Three Problems, Same Fix¶

The picture had three problems, and so does the clip.

  • Too many weights. A few seconds across several axes is already hundreds of numbers. A plain network ties a weight to every one.
  • It can happen anywhere. The activity can start at any moment in the window, just as the letter could sit anywhere in the image.
  • Neighbors look alike. Two readings a fraction of a second apart are nearly identical, so one number on its own says almost nothing.

The fix is the same filter, slid along the clip. One dimension instead of two: time.

The Filter Slides Across Time¶

In the paper the convolution and pooling filters run along the time axis, one sensor channel at a time. A filter is a short strip of weights — here 5 readings wide. Lay it over the start of the signal, multiply, add, write down one number. Slide it forward and do it again.

The row of numbers it leaves behind is the feature map, and it lights up wherever the signal has the little shape the filter is looking for, no matter when that shape happens.

The Whole Machine¶

Stack a few of these and you have the paper's CNN.

  • A Conv1D layer slides many filters across the window, each followed by ReLU, max pooling and normalization
  • A second and third convolution read patterns made of the earlier layers' patterns, at coarser time scales
  • A unification layer then ties together the separate sensor channels into one shared representation
  • A softmax maps that onto the activity classes

Same ingredients as the image CNN, plus one new piece — the layer that unifies the channels. Conv2d becomes Conv1D; the grid becomes a clip.

In Keras¶

from tensorflow.keras.models import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Conv1D, MaxPooling1D, Flatten, Dense

model = Sequential([
    Conv1D(50, 5, activation="relu", input_shape=(32, 5)),  # time steps, sensor channels
    MaxPooling1D(2),

    Conv1D(40, 5, activation="relu"),
    MaxPooling1D(2),

    Conv1D(20, 3, activation="relu"),

    Flatten(),
    Dense(400, activation="relu"),        # unify the sensor channels
    Dense(12, activation="softmax"),      # activity classes
])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
              metrics=["accuracy"])

A handful of lines. Swap Conv2d for Conv1D and the image CNN becomes a motion CNN.

Case Study: From Door Handles to Tennis Swings¶

The authors tested the same CNN on two very different motion datasets: one of whole-body activity around a kitchen — opening doors, drawers and the fridge, drinking from a cup — and one of hand gestures, from stirring a bowl to a tennis forehand, backhand and smash.

Both share the hard part: a brief, meaningful motion has to be picked out of a long stream that is mostly the "Null" class — ordinary movement that means nothing.

What the Study Found¶

Against four baselines — an SVM, nearest-neighbor, hand-crafted mean-and-variance features, and a deep belief network — the CNN came out on top on both datasets, across every metric.

On the hand-gesture data it reached about 95 percent accuracy, and on the hardest subjects it beat the best hand-crafted-feature baseline by roughly 5 points. Because the filters are learned rather than designed by hand, the same network transfers from one activity set to the other.

Learned Filters, Not Hand-Crafted Features¶

The older methods lived or died by the features a person chose — the mean, the variance, a Fourier transform of each window. The CNN skips that step: the convolution filters are learned from the labels, so they tune themselves to whatever shape actually separates the activities.

That the CNN also beats the deep belief network — a deep model trained without the labels — is the paper's quiet point: for this problem, learning the filters under supervision is what carries the signal.

Why It Is the Same Machine¶

An activity is a small, local shape in the motion that can land anywhere in the window. That is exactly what a sliding filter is built to find.

The O and the X were shapes in space; a door pull or a tennis swing is a shape in time. One fewer dimension, the same idea — a filter that slides, a feature map, ReLU, pooling — plus one new step that unifies the separate sensor channels.

Key Ideas¶

  • A filter is a small square of weights slid across the picture. Multiply, add, add a bias: a feature map
  • ReLU, then max pooling: keep the largest value in each block. Fewer inputs, and a small shift leaves the answer alone
  • The pooled grid becomes a column into an ordinary network, trained by backpropagation with cross entropy. 36 pixels became 4 inputs
  • The filter reads neighbors together, which is what pixels one at a time cannot do
  • Color is three channels. A filter is three grids and one bias. Gray throws the color away
  • Many filters make many maps, and those maps are the next layer's channels
  • nn.Conv2d, nn.MaxPool2d, nn.Linear
  • In economics the CNN is mostly a measuring device: it turns pictures into numbers that a regression then uses
